report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is supported, though the average benefit appears modest and evidence certainty is moderate rather than definitive.

The key direct evidence is a large randomized trial in cesarean delivery that found chlorhexidine–alcohol produced a significantly lower 30-day rate of superficial or deep surgical-site infection than iodine–alcohol. https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048

Evidence synthesis agrees: a cesarean-specific systematic review/meta-analysis concluded that chlorhexidine–alcohol reduces surgical-site infection compared with povidone–iodine preparations. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30184558/ More recent pooled randomized-trial evidence estimates a relative risk of 0.69 (95% CI 0.54–0.89)—about a 31% relative reduction—with no important observed statistical heterogeneity. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12675439/

However, not every individual trial has found a statistically significant difference, and comparative studies may use different iodine formulations (aqueous vs alcohol-based), chlorhexidine concentrations, and patient populations. A Cochrane review therefore characterizes the result more cautiously: chlorhexidine gluconate is *probably slightly more effective* than povidone–iodine at preventing post-cesarean surgical-site infection (moderate-certainty evidence). https://www.cochrane.org/CD007462/PREG_skin-preparation-preventing-infection-following-caesarean-section

Thus, when both products are appropriate and used correctly on intact skin, chlorhexidine–alcohol is a reasonable preferred preparation for lowering cesarean wound-infection risk. Product labeling, drying time/fire safety, chlorhexidine allergy, and avoiding inappropriate use near mucosal or neonatal tissue remain important.
